source_text: Ἐδίδαξε δὲ ἡμᾶς ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ ὅστις ἦν ὁ πέμψας ἐν τῷ „οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα. εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱὸς,“ καὶ τῷ „θεὸν οὐδεὶς ἑώρακε πώποτε· καὶ μονογενής γε ὢν θεὸς. ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρὸς, ἐκεῖνος ἐξηγήσατο,“ ἐκεῖνος θεολογῶν ἀπήγγειλε τὰ περὶ θεοῦ τοῖς γνησίοις αὐτοῦ μαθηταῖς· ὧν ἴχνη ἐν τοῖς γεγραμμένοις εὑρίσκοντες ἀφορμὰς ἔχομεν θεολογεῖν. ὅπου μὲν ἀκούοντες· „ὁ θεὸς φῶς ἐστι, καὶ σκοτία οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτῷ οὐδεμία.“ ὅπου δέ· „πνεῦμα ὁ θεὸς, καὶ τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας αὐτὸν ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ δεῖ προσκυνεῖν.“ ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐφ᾿ οἷς ἔπεμψεν αὐτὸν ὁ πατὴρ μυρία ἐστὶν. ἅτινα ὁ βουλόμενος μανθανέτω, πῇ μὲν ἀπὸ τῶν προκηρυξάντων περὶ αὐτοῦ προφητῶν πῇ δ᾿ ἀπὸ τῶν εὐαγγελιστῶν· οὐκ ὀλίγα δ᾿ εἴσεται καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀποστόλων καὶ μάλιστα Παύλου. ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς μὲν εὐσεβοῦντας οὗτος φωταγωγεῖ τοὺς δὲ ἁμαρτάνοντας κολάσει, ὅπερ οὐκ ἰδὼν ὁ Κέλσος πεποίηκε· καὶ τοὺς μἐν εὐσεβοῦντας φωταγωγήσων τοὺς δὲ ἁμαρτάνοντας ἢ μεταγνόντας ἐλεήσων.
pass_a_gloss: Jesus taught (διδάσκω) us also who was the one having sent (πέμπω) [him], in the 'no one knew (γινώσκω) the Father (πατήρ) except the Son (υἱός)', and in the 'God (θεός) no one has seen (ὁράω) ever (πώποτε); and indeed being only-begotten God (μονογενὴς θεός), the one being into the bosom (κόλπος) of the Father, that one has expounded/made known (ἐξηγέομαι).' That one, theologizing (θεολογέω, speaking of God), announced (ἀπαγγέλλω) the things about God to his genuine (γνήσιος) disciples (μαθητής); of which finding traces (ἴχνος) in the writings (τὰ γεγραμμένα) we have starting-points (ἀφορμή) to theologize: where hearing 'God is light (φῶς), and darkness (σκοτία) is not in him, none (οὐδεμία)'; and where 'God [is] spirit (πνεῦμα), and those worshiping (προσκυνέω) him must (δεῖ) worship in spirit and truth (ἀλήθεια).' But also the things for which (ἐφ' οἷς) the Father sent him are myriad/countless (μυρία); which let the one wishing learn (μανθάνω), in part from the prophets (προφήτης) who proclaimed-beforehand (προκηρύσσω) about him, in part from the evangelists (εὐαγγελιστής); and not few things he will know also from the apostles (ἀπόστολος), and especially Paul. But also this one enlightens/leads-to-light (φωταγωγέω) the pious (εὐσεβέω) and will punish (κολάζω, fut.) the sinning (ἁμαρτάνω), which not having seen Celsus has made/written (ποιέω): 'and about to enlighten (fut. ptc. of purpose) the pious, and about to have mercy (ἐλεέω) on the sinning or having repented (μεταγιγνώσκω).'
pass_b_english: Jesus also taught us who it was that sent him, in the words “No one has known the Father except the Son” (Matthew 11:27; compare Luke 10:22), and in “No one has ever seen God; and he who is indeed the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known” (John 1:18). It was he who, speaking of God, declared to his true disciples what concerns God; and since we find traces of this in the Scriptures, we have starting points for speaking about God. In one place we hear, “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5); in another, “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).

Moreover, the purposes for which the Father sent him are countless. Let anyone who wishes learn them, partly from the prophets who proclaimed him beforehand, partly from the evangelists; and he will learn not a few things from the apostles as well, and above all from Paul. Further, he gives light to the godly and will punish sinners. Celsus did not see this when he wrote: “and to give light to the godly, and to have mercy on those who sin or who have repented.”

choices.why: 'He, speaking of God, declared the truths about God' made 'It was he who, speaking of God, declared ... what concerns God' (τὰ περὶ θεοῦ; 'truths' was an addition)

2.71: Celsus's closing words 'to have mercy on those who sin or who have repented' (ἢ μεταγνόντας) may be damaged in the staged text. It is translated as given, with a note added. Passed, but the owner may want to compare it against the Koetschau apparatus.

translator_notes: The chapter answers Celsus’s challenge about the sender implied in the messenger question of 2.70. Matthew 11:27 is quoted loosely (NT: οὐδὲ τὸν πατέρα τις ἐπιγινώσκει εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός; Luke 10:22: τίς ἐστιν ὁ πατὴρ εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός). John 1:18 is quoted with the reading μονογενὴς θεός and an added emphatic καὶ... γε ὤν (‘he who is indeed’), kept. 1 John 1:5 and John 4:24 agree with the NT apart from word order. ‘God is spirit’ is lowercase because it names God’s nature, not the Holy Spirit. κολάσει is taken as the future of κολάζω (‘will punish’), parallel to φωταγωγεῖ; it could be read as the dative noun (‘by punishment’), which would not change the sense much. The closing words are Celsus’s, quoted as Origen gives them: future participles of purpose (‘to give light... to have mercy’); ἢ μεταγνόντας rendered ‘or who have repented’. Origen’s point is that Celsus mentions light and mercy but leaves out punishment. The fuller context of Celsus’s sentence is not given here; no connective has been supplied, and the staged text may be damaged at this point.
